q: Why use a button element instead of a clickable div for an action?
a: A native button supplies action semantics and standard keyboard behavior; a div requires that behavior to be built and tested.
explanation: Include accessible naming, focus visibility, and appropriate disabled behavior. Native semantics reduce work but do not excuse poor labels or unreachable controls.
mistake: Adding a click handler and considering accessibility finished.
followups: When should an anchor be used?

q: A modal looks correct but keyboard focus moves behind it. What is missing?
a: Modal interaction needs deliberate focus entry, containment while open, and return to the triggering control.
explanation: Use appropriate dialog semantics and test escape/close behavior and assistive technologies. Hiding content visually is not enough to define keyboard interaction.
mistake: Treating a high z-index as a complete modal implementation.

q: Users see stale frontend assets after a release. How do you design caching?
a: Use content-versioned asset URLs and appropriate cache directives, while giving the entry document a deliberate freshness policy.
explanation: Cache behavior involves browsers, CDNs, and service workers. Identify the layer serving old data before changing headers. Personal data needs a different policy from public static assets.
mistake: Disabling all caching instead of diagnosing the stale layer.

q: Design a form with async validation and accessible errors.
a: Keep field values and validation state clear, associate errors with fields, and validate again at the server boundary.
explanation: Prevent stale validation responses from overwriting newer input. Preserve typed data on failure and guide focus appropriately after submission. Client validation improves feedback, not server trust.
mistake: Treating client-side validation as a security boundary.
followups: How do you announce a form-level error?

q: A web app loads megabytes of JavaScript before showing its main workflow. What would you change?
a: Measure critical-path assets and user interactions, then split unnecessary code and defer suitable work.
explanation: Account for parsing and execution on slow devices as well as transfer size. Prefetch only with evidence and monitor failures at loading boundaries. Keep essential controls usable early.
mistake: Optimizing bundle size while ignoring main-thread execution cost.
followups: What would you test on a slow device?

q: Navigating quickly between records sometimes displays the wrong record. How do you reason about this?
a: Tie each response to the active record/request and prevent obsolete responses from changing the current view.
explanation: Cancellation helps but should not be the only guard. Model loading and errors per request, avoid sharing unrelated cache keys, and reproduce deliberately reversed response order.
mistake: Assuming responses arrive in navigation order.

q: Several frontend teams build incompatible controls. How would you improve the shared platform?
a: Define accessible contracts and contribution ownership, then deliver reusable components with measured adoption and migration support.
explanation: Validate real product workflows and avoid forcing every exceptional interaction into one component. Establish versioning, compatibility checks, and an escalation path for product-specific needs.
mistake: Equating shared code with consistent user behavior.

q: Would independently deployed frontend modules help a large organization?
a: Compare team autonomy with integration, dependency, performance, and user-experience costs before choosing boundaries.
explanation: Define routing, authentication, shared design contracts, and failure containment. A modular monolith may meet the need with less operational cost. Pilot a boundary with objective delivery metrics.
mistake: Adopting micro frontends solely because many teams exist.
followups: What happens when one module fails?
